translations.text: The Jewish brothers in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea send greetings to our Jewish brothers in Egypt. Peace and grace be with you.
May God be good to you and remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May he give all of you a heart to fear him and to carry out his commandments wholeheartedly and with a willing spirit.
May he open your ears and your hearts to his laws and his commandments, and establish peace with you.
May he hear your petition, be reconciled to you, and not abandon you in times of trouble.
And now, here we are, praying for you.

In the year one hundred and sixty-nine, during the reign of Demetrius, we Jews wrote to you amid the troubles and afflictions that had befallen us during these years, since Jason and those with him were sent from the kingdom to the holy land.
They burned the gates and shed innocent blood. We prayed and pleaded with the Lord, and he heard our voice. We offered sacrifices and fine flour, lit the lamps, and set out the bread of the Presence.
And now you are to celebrate the Festival of Shelters in December.

In the year one hundred and eighty-eight, those in Jerusalem and Judea and all the elders of Judea send greetings and good health to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, who belongs to the family of the anointed priests, and to the Jews in Egypt.
We give abundant and heartfelt thanks to God, who stood by us and rescued us from all the afflictions that came upon us.
For when the king came against us in war to attack the holy city,

He drove him away and cast him into Persia. For when he went there with his entire army, he who was thought to be invincible was killed in the temple of Nanaea, whose priests cunningly seized them and shut them in.
For Antiochus and his friends had gone there so that he might live with her and receive great wealth as a dowry.
The priests of Nanaea acted deceitfully and made promises to him. But when he entered within the temple wall with a few men,
they opened a small door and came in upon him. They threw stones at him and killed him, cut off his head, and threw it to those outside.
But blessed in everything is our God, who handed over the wicked.

Since we are about to celebrate the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth of December, we wish to inform you as well, so that you too may celebrate it like the Festival of Shelters. We will also tell you about the fire, when Nehemiah built the temple and the altar and offered sacrifices.

When our ancestors were going to Persia, the righteous priests of that time secretly took some of the fire from the altar and hid it in a well that had no water. They concealed it so that no one would know its location.
After many years had passed, when it pleased God, Nehemiah was sent by the king of Persia with the descendants of the priests who had hidden the fire.

He sent them to bring the fire. They came back and said that they had found no fire, but only muddy water. He ordered them to take some of it and bring it. When the sacrifices and offerings had been laid out, Nehemiah ordered the priests to sprinkle some of it on the wood and on the sacrifices.
When they had done this and a little time had passed, the sun shone out, having previously been obscured by clouds. Then a great fire blazed up, so that everyone was amazed.
The priests stood in prayer until the fire had finished its work. When the priests, Jonathan, and the rest came down, they said that it had been kindled through Nehemiah’s prayer.
His prayer was as follows: “Lord, Lord, God Almighty and Creator of all, awesome and mighty, righteous and merciful, you alone are king, and you alone are kind,
you alone are the sustainer, the righteous one who lives forever and rules over all, Israel’s deliverer from every evil, who chose our ancestors and made them holy.
Accept this offering on behalf of all your people Israel, and protect and sanctify your portion and your inheritance.
Gather our scattered people and free those enslaved among the unclean and hateful nations. Look upon us, so that the nations may know that you are our God.”
Punish those who exalt themselves and arrogantly enslave others.
Establish your people firmly in your holy place, as Moses said.
Meanwhile, the priests stood singing songs of praise.
When the sacrifices and offerings were completed, Nehemiah ordered that the remaining water be set down and that the place be surrounded with large stones.
When they did this, a flame of fire blazed until the light of the fire on the altar had died away.

When the matter became known and it was revealed to the king of Persia that muddy water had been found at the place where those taken captive had hidden the fire, and that Nehemiah and those with him had used it to consecrate the offerings and sacrifices,
The king built up the place and made a temple there after investigating the matter.
the king gave them great and valuable gifts. They received them and gave them to those who were in need.
Nehemiah's people called it Gonaphthar, which means “purification,” but among many people it is called Nephthai.
It is found in the book of Jeremiah the prophet that he commanded those who came afterward to take fire, as it shows.

The prophet, who gave them the law, instructed those who came afterward not to forget the Lord’s commandments or let their minds be turned aside when they saw gold and silver idols and their adornment.
He said other things like these and urged them not to remove the law from their hearts.

It was also written in the book that, in accordance with what had been revealed to him, the prophet commanded that the ark and the tabernacle should go with him. When he went out to the mountain that Moses had climbed to see the Lord’s inheritance,
Jeremiah came and found a chamber in a cave. He entered and placed the tabernacle, the ark, and the incense altar there, and blocked up the entrance.
Some of those who had gone with him went out to identify the path and the place, but they could not find them.
When Jeremiah learned of it, he rebuked them and said that the place would remain unknown until God gathered the congregation of the people and showed them mercy.
Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the glory of the Lord and the cloud will appear, as it used to appear over Moses, and as Solomon also asked that the place be magnificently consecrated.
It was related that, in keeping with the wisdom he possessed, he offered offerings and sacrifices for the dedication and completion of the temple.
Just as Moses prayed to the Lord, and fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifices and offerings, so Solomon also prayed, and fire came down and consumed the sacrifices and burnt offerings.
For Moses had said, “Because the [?] of the sin offering was not eaten, the fire consumed it.”
Likewise, Solomon also observed eight days.

It was also related in the writings and memoirs of Nehemiah that he acted in this way: he gathered and arranged the books about the kingdoms, the prophets, and David, and the letters of kings concerning offerings and sacrifices.
In the same way, Judas also gathered together all the things that had been scattered because of the wars that befell us, and they are here with us.
Therefore, if you need any of them, send for them and obtain them for yourselves.
Since we are about to celebrate the purification, we have also written to you so that you too may celebrate it.
But God, who delivered his people in every circumstance and gave everyone an inheritance, kingship, priesthood, and holiness,

as he promised through the law—he is the one in whom we hope, that he will soon have mercy on us and gather us from under heaven to his holy place. For he has rescued us from many evils and has also purified the place.
Now concerning Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, the purification of the great and glorious temple, and the dedication of the altar,
and also concerning the wars that took place against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator;

and the wonders that were visibly performed from heaven for those who fought bravely on behalf of the Jews, so that, although they were few in number, they pursued and scattered all the nations of the lands that came against them with arrogance and insolence,

so that the temple and the sanctuary, renowned throughout the earth, came to enjoy quiet and rest, the city was freed from subjection to the nations, and they gathered and restored the laws that were on the verge of being swept away, through the Lord's will and his mercy toward them—
all these events, which were written down in five books by Jason of Cyrene, we have undertaken, with great effort, to write in abbreviated form in one book.

For we saw the overwhelming abundance of words and the difficulty faced by those who wish to investigate the accounts of the events and the lengthy narrative, because of the sheer amount of material related.

We therefore undertook the labor of arranging it and setting it out briefly, so that we might strengthen the souls of readers in the truth, so that those who wish to retain a careful memory of the account might grasp it easily, and so that its usefulness might be clearly apparent to everyone who reads it.

For us, however, who undertook these matters and wrote them in abbreviated form, this was not easy. Rather, with sweat, toil, weariness, and much sleeplessness, we compared, arranged, and wrote them in abbreviated form.

For just as someone who wishes to arrange and prepare a banquet and provide comfort for many does not find it easy himself, but gladly accepts toil and weariness because he wishes to give comfort and pleasure to those he has invited, so we too, for the pleasure and comfort of many, gladly accepted toil and weariness and endured much hardship.
We have therefore refrained from writing out all the histories, and we wish, with diligence and great effort, to relate briefly the things that have been written and told at length.

For just as a master builder, when building a house, concerns himself with the entire plan of the building, while the one who paints and decorates it with colors inquires into and seeks everything needed for the decoration of the house, so I think it is with us.
For examining and investigating everything and writing it all down together is required of the one who begins the work.
To pursue brevity of expression and refrain from lengthy treatment is appropriate for someone who relates much in few words in an abridgment.

From here, then, let us begin the accounts mentioned above and put together in abbreviated form. For it is good to give an extensive explanation and make matters clear before the narrative, but to tell the narrative itself briefly.
When the holy city was living in quiet and peace, and the laws were being faithfully observed because of the righteousness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of evil,
even kings came to honor the temple and the place with honors and great and splendid offerings.
even Seleucus, king of Asia, provided from his own resources everything needed for the service of the offerings.
But Simon, who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and had been appointed administrator of the temple, rose up against the priests, for he supported the wrongdoing taking place in the city.
When he could not overcome Onias the high priest, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was the ruler and governor of Syria and Phoenicia.

He informed him about the treasury in the temple in Jerusalem, telling him that the wealth in it was immeasurable and beyond counting. He said that all this should not be reckoned as funds for sacrifices and offerings, but should be placed under the king’s authority.

Apollonius went and informed the king about the treasury and the wealth that had been reported to him. The king summoned Heliodorus, who had been appointed over his affairs, and commissioned him and sent him to take and bring back all the treasure and wealth he had been told about.
Heliodorus immediately set out and traveled through the cities of Syria and Phoenicia, hurrying to carry out and complete the king’s command.

When Heliodorus arrived in Jerusalem, he was received with great honor by the high priest and the city. He explained to them the matter on which he had been sent, which had been reported to the king, and asked them whether these things were really so.
The high priest explained to him that these were deposits held for orphans and widows,

Some of it belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, an honored and wealthy man. It was not as the wicked Simon had come and said in his slanderous accusation. The total amounted to four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold.

Those who had trusted in the holiness of the place, the sanctity of the temple, and its great and glorious reputation throughout the world—that it would not be plundered or robbed—could not be wronged and deprived of their property.
But Heliodorus, because of the king’s command, said that these funds had to be brought into the royal treasury and deposited there.
He appointed a day for them when he would go in, inspect the funds, and take control of them. There was no small distress throughout the city.
The priests, in their priestly robes, threw themselves on the ground, crying out and appealing to the one who had established the law for them that deposits should be kept intact for their owners.
Moreover, the hearts of all who saw the high priest melted, for the appearance of his face and his changed expression revealed the anguish of his soul.
For grace was poured out upon the man and rested on him, and beauty of appearance rested upon his body. Because of this, the painful suffering within his soul became apparent.
People also came out of their houses in crowds, praying and pleading that the temple would not become an object of laughter and mockery.

Women, with sackcloth tied around their waists, wandered through the streets. Of the young women who had been kept indoors, some ran to the gates, some to the wall, and some peered out through the windows.
They all stretched out their hands, crying out and pleading with the one who dwells in heaven.
It was a sight that would move anyone to pity at the people’s anguish and distress, and at the high priest’s struggle, suffering, and anxious waiting.
They all cried out and appealed to God, who rules over all, that the things entrusted to them might be kept intact, with every precaution, for those who had entrusted them.
But Heliodorus was pressing ahead to accomplish the business for which he had come.

He began to enter the treasury with the armed men and soldiers who were with him. Immediately the Lord of spirits, the God of every power and every authority, appeared and showed them a wonder and a great revelation, so that all who had dared to enter lost their strength and fell down in amazement at the power of God that had appeared to them.

For a terrifying horse appeared to them, ridden by a man of very handsome appearance, splendid in the clothing wrapped around him. It came charging and caused terror before Heliodorus with the clattering sound of its armor. Its rider appeared to be equipped with golden armor.

Two other young men also appeared with him, handsome in appearance, splendid in strength, and magnificent and astonishing in their clothing. They stood on either side of Heliodorus and beat him with heavy blows.
Suddenly he fell to the ground, with deep darkness enveloping him. They picked him up and carried him outside into the courtyard.
The man who only a little earlier had been entering the treasury with arrogance and great power now lay helpless, unable to help himself. The power of God had been clearly revealed.
They left him lying there, stricken by the power of justice, with neither hope nor expectation of life.

But the people blessed the Lord, who had brought glory to his place. The temple, which only a little earlier had been full of fear and alarm, was filled with delight and joy through the action and revelation of the Lord who rules over all.
Immediately some of Heliodorus’s friends approached and begged Onias to pray and ask the Lord to grant life to the man who lay there utterly without hope.
The high priest considered that the king might perhaps suppose that something had happened to Heliodorus through some action by the Jews, so he offered sacrifices for the man’s life.

While the high priest was standing and making atonement for him, those same young men appeared again to Heliodorus in the same clothes as before. They said to him, “Be very grateful to Onias the high priest, for it is because of him that the Lord has given you your life.
Now that you have been scourged by God, go and proclaim to everyone his greatness and his mighty dominion.” When they had said these things to him, they were no longer seen.

Heliodorus offered sacrifices to God, pleaded with him, and offered a great prayer before him because he had given him his life. He also honored Onias greatly. Then he returned to the king with his entire force.
He testified and told everyone about the deeds and power of the mighty God who had appeared to him before his own eyes.
The king questioned Heliodorus about what had happened and wanted to send someone to Jerusalem once again. Heliodorus said to him,

“If you have anyone who has wronged you and is an enemy of your interests, send him there. You will receive him back scourged and tortured, if he even survives, because the power of God truly is in that place.
For the one whose dwelling is in heaven watches over and guards that place. Those who go there to harm it, he tortures, scourges, and destroys.”
This is how matters stood concerning Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury.

But that wicked Simon, whom we mentioned earlier, who had been the informer and betrayer of the city and the treasury, slandered Onias and made accusations against him, as though he had caused what happened to Heliodorus and was responsible for all the evils that had come upon him.
He even dared to say that the man who had done good for his city, cared for his fellow countrymen, and been zealous for the law was responsible for all the evils.
The evil arising from his hostility grew so great that many murders were committed by those whom Simon incited.
Onias therefore saw this malicious envy, and saw Apollonius, the chief official and governor of Syria and Phoenicia, stirring up trouble, supporting Simon, and adding to his wickedness.
It even reached the king’s ears that he was a slanderer and a betrayer of his fellow citizens. Onias therefore considered and reflected on how help might come to his people.

He understood and saw that he had no further means of securing peace unless God’s mercy willed it, that matters could not be put right apart from God, and that Simon would not cease his wickedness and troublemaking unless help came from heaven.

After King Seleucus died and Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, succeeded him as king, Jason, the brother of Onias the high priest, went and deceitfully obtained authority over the high priesthood from the king.
He promised to give him three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from other revenues.

He also promised to give another hundred and fifty if the king would permit him to build a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to Greek custom, establish an athletic competition in which people would compete in the stadium, and register the inhabitants of Jerusalem as Antiochenes.
When the king gave him permission and he unjustly obtained the high priesthood and leadership, he immediately, in his wickedness, turned all his fellow countrymen toward pagan ways of thinking.

He also removed and abolished the arrangements established for the Jews through God’s mercy, which had been secured through John, the father of Eupolemus, who went as an envoy to the Romans concerning peace. He dismantled the true religious observances and laws, and established and introduced wicked laws and customs.
For he diligently and hurriedly established a gymnasium beneath the city wall, subjected the physically strong to his authority, and made them pass under the measuring line.
Such was the zeal for paganism, the folly of adopting Greek ways, and the error of the nations brought about by the wicked Jason, who was no high priest. In this way defilement increased,

so that the priests no longer cared about service at the altar, sacrifices, and offerings. Instead, they despised the temple and its service and hurried to watch and enjoy the lawless competition and the [?] of the wrestling contest.
They despised the honor of their ancestors’ worship and desired the empty glory of pagan practices.

For this reason disaster overtook them. Those whose practices they envied, and whom they wanted to imitate in everything, turned against them and became their enemies. At their hands they were punished according to their deeds.
For it is neither good nor right for anyone to violate the holy laws. But each day, in its own time, makes these things known.
When the athletic competition held once every five years took place in Tyre, the king also came there to watch.

Jason, the abominable and unclean man, sent spectators from Jerusalem who were Antiochenes. Through them he sent three thousand three hundred in silver to be taken for the sacrifice to Hercules that was being held there. But those who carried the money pleaded and urged that it should not be used for the sacrifice, because this was not right, and they assigned it to the expenses of other matters.
But because of the man who had sent it for this purpose, and because of those who urged that they use it in this way, it happened that it was put to ordinary use for another service.

When Apollonius son of Menestheus was sent to Egypt to King Philometor of Egypt concerning special honors, Antiochus concluded in his mind that Philometor had become hostile to the affairs of his kingdom, and he took precautions for his own safety. For this reason he came to Joppa on business, and from there he went up to Jerusalem.
He was received with great honor and praise by Jason and by the city, with praise and shouting. Afterward he set out from there for Phoenicia.
After three years Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the wicked Simon, to carry to the king the gifts he had promised to give him, and to speak to him about important matters that they needed.
When he went, he presented himself before the king and won his praise. He asked for the high priesthood, outbid Jason, and gave three hundred additional talents of silver.
After receiving the king's command, he returned, although he had done nothing worthy of the high priesthood. Instead, he was clothed in fury and anger and was full of reckless and arrogant thoughts.
As for Jason, who had plotted against his own brother, another man now plotted against him, and he fled to the land of Ammon.
Menelaus held the position of authority, but he did not have the means to pay what he had promised the king.

Sostratus, who had been appointed governor over the citadel, came and demanded payment from him, for he had been given authority to collect the payments for important matters. For this reason both men were summoned before the king.
Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as high priest in his place, while Sostratus left Crates, who had been appointed over the Cypriots.
While they were occupied with these matters, the people of Tarsus and Mallus happened to revolt because Antioch had been given as a gift to the king's concubine.
As soon as the king heard, he came to pacify them. He left there the man who was acting in place of Andronicus, who had been appointed over important affairs.

Menelaus, thinking that he had found an opportunity, stole some of the gold vessels from the temple and gave them to Andronicus. It was discovered that he had sent the rest away and sold them in Tyre and the surrounding cities.
When Onias learned this for certain, he rebuked him, then withdrew and went to Daphne, which is beside Antioch.

For this reason Menelaus went secretly to Andronicus and asked him to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias and deceitfully spoke words of peace to him. With an oath and assurances, he gave them his right hand and persuaded Onias to come out of the sanctuary. He came out with doubts in his mind, and as soon as he came out, Andronicus killed him, showing no regard for his righteousness.
For this reason not only the Jews reviled and denounced him, but many of the Gentiles also insulted and denounced him over the unjust killing of the man.

When the king returned from the regions of Cilicia, the Jews in all the cities complained to him about the injustice committed in the killing of Onias. Many Gentiles also supported them, because they were deeply distressed over the unlawful killing of Onias.
When King Antiochus heard, he was grieved to his very soul and wept bitterly. He was completely overcome by sorrow over the death of this righteous, chaste, humble, peaceable, and kind man.

He became intensely angry and ordered them to strip Andronicus of his purple robes, tear his clothes, and lead him around the whole city. In the very place where he had wronged Onias, he put the wicked man to death. Thus the Lord repaid him with the punishment he deserved.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem gathered within the city against Lysimachus, with Menelaus's approval, and demanded from him the large amount of gold he had taken. When the news spread outside, many people came against Lysimachus.

When Lysimachus saw that the crowds were becoming agitated and angry with him, he armed about three thousand men and began killing with his wicked hands. His assistant and the leader of the murderers was an unclean and abominable man who was advanced in years and far gone in his thinking.

When they saw Lysimachus's treachery and wickedness, they took stones and clubs, and some took ashes, and they brought terror and confusion upon those who were with Lysimachus and upon his supporters.
They killed many of them and knocked some of them to the ground, while the rest fled. They killed the temple robber himself beside the treasury.
Over these matters, Menelaus stood against them in court.
When the king came to Tyre, the three men sent by the elders of the assembly pleaded their case before him.
When Menelaus saw that he was losing his case, he promised Ptolemy many gifts to persuade the king on his behalf.
Ptolemy took the king aside, separating him from them for a little while as though to let him rest, and changed his mind.

He acquitted Menelaus, who was responsible for all these evils, of the charges brought by his accusers. But he condemned those unfortunate, poor men to death, even though they would have been acquitted if they had pleaded their case before the Scythians.
Immediately, the citizens undertook to bear the losses caused by injustice on behalf of the city, the people, and the sacred vessels.
For this reason, even the Tyrians were deeply distressed by the unjust judgment through which he had killed these men without cause. The Tyrians themselves took them and buried them with great honor.

Menelaus sent to collect the compensation for the oppression that he had promised. He grew more arrogant and more entrenched in his wickedness, becoming a great adversary to the citizens of his own city.
At this same time Antiochus went to Egypt for the second time.
For about forty days, throughout the whole city, horsemen were seen racing through the air, dressed in golden robes, holding spears, and equipped with every kind of weapon.

They spurred their horses and raced back and forth, waving their shields and drawing their swords. Their bows were drawn, and they wore armor and were equipped with every kind of golden weapon of war. They all shone and flashed together.
All the people pleaded and prayed that this vision would turn out for good.

A false report spread that Antiochus had died. Jason took about a thousand men and suddenly attacked the city. He pressed the attack fiercely against the city, and most of the people fled and climbed onto the wall, because the city was close to being lost. Menelaus fled up to the citadel.

Jason slaughtered the citizens of his own city. The wicked man did not consider or understand that his joy was full of distress and deep mourning, because he was waging war and carrying out slaughter among his own people and his own kin.
Although he did all these things, he could not seize power. Instead, his venture ended in disgrace, and he gave up and fled again to the land of Ammon.

His final end was evil and bitter. Aretas, king of the Arabs, plotted against him, and he escaped from there and fled from city to city. Everyone pursued him as a rebel against the law, and they despised and scorned him as a betrayer of his city and his people. In great disgrace he fled to Egypt.

Like refuse thrown out of a house, he was thrown out of his own country and perished in Lacedaemon, in a foreign land. He had gone there as though to his own relatives, to find shelter with them, and he died there.
He was not granted burial in his ancestors’ tomb, nor weeping, nor mourning, nor any of the rites with which people are buried.

They sent word to the king about everything that had happened. He thought that Judea intended to rebel, so he hurried from Egypt, filled with rage and fury, and killed many people in the city with the sword.
He had ordered his soldiers to kill without mercy everyone who fell into their hands. They even entered the houses and killed people.
There was slaughter of old men, boys, young men, and young women, and the destruction of sons, daughters, and little infants.
Thus, within three days about eighty thousand people were lost and destroyed: forty thousand were killed, and forty thousand were sold into slavery.

All this was not enough for the king. He also dared to enter the great and holy temple, renowned throughout the whole earth. His guide was Menelaus, who had become a betrayer of the law and his own country.

With his unclean hands he took the sacred vessels, including those given by other kings and those deposited by cities for the glory, grandeur, and honor of the temple. With his defiled hands he took everything in its sanctuary and all its treasures and gave them to them.

Antiochus became proud and arrogant in his thinking. He did not consider or understand that, because of the sins of the city’s inhabitants, the Lord had been angry for a short time and had withdrawn his watchful care from the place.

For if they had not been caught up in many sins, they would not have suffered and endured these things. It would have been as it was with Heliodorus, who was sent by King Seleucus to the wealth in the treasury: when he tried to enter the treasury, a bitter scourge was sent upon him, and he returned with his proud spirit humbled.
For the people did not exist for the sake of the place; rather, the Lord chose the place for the sake of the people.

For this reason, the place itself shared with the people in the punishment for their wicked deeds. Later, when deliverance came from the Lord, it also shared in the blessings. The temple, which had been abandoned in God's anger, was restored in great glory by the will of the Most High.

Antiochus took eighteen hundred talents from the temple and hurried away to Antioch. In his arrogance he thought he could turn the land into sea and the sea into dry land, because he had become so conceited and proud in his thinking.

He left governors who mistreated our people. In Jerusalem he left Philip, who was Phrygian by birth and whose disposition was impure, tyrannical, and more loathsome than that of the man who had appointed him.

At Gerizim he left Andronicus. Along with them he left Menelaus, who was even more arrogant and conceited than they were and mistreated his fellow citizens. Antiochus was filled with anger and bitter hostility toward the Jews.
He sent Apollonius, the chief of all the unclean, with an army of twenty-two thousand, ordering them to kill those who were old and advanced in years and to sell the women and young people.
When this man arrived in Jerusalem, he deceitfully spoke peaceful words to them and waited until the holy Sabbath day. When he found the Jews resting from work, he armed everyone who was with him.
He ordered them to kill everyone who came outside the city as though to watch a spectacle. He also rushed into the city, armed along with his army, and killed many people.

But Judas Maccabeus withdrew with nine others who were with him and went into the wilderness. They lived like wild animals in the mountains, sustaining themselves on roots and plants from the ground so that they would not share in the defilement.
A short time later, the king sent another man, an Athenian, to force the Jews to transgress the laws and commandments of their ancestors and to stop living according to God's laws.

They were also to defile the temple in Jerusalem and call it the temple of Baal-shamayn Olympios, and to call the one at Gerizim the temple of Baal-shamayn Xenios, in keeping with the inhabitants of that place.
The distress and oppression that all of them suffered were terrible and bitter.

For the temple was filled with the revelry, music, and festivities of the gentiles, and they treated it with great contempt. They also had intercourse with women all around it, and brought things that were forbidden inside the temple.
The altar, which had been prepared for the offerings prescribed in the law, was entirely filled with pollution and uncleanness.
The oppression was such that no one could keep the Sabbath or celebrate and observe an ancestral festival, or even acknowledge and say that he was a Jew.

Every month, on the days celebrating the king's birth, they were brought under bitter compulsion to offer sacrifices. There was also a festival of Dionysus, and they forced them to carry branches, march around, and take part in the festivities on the day of Dionysus.
He also sent an order to the neighboring gentile cities and to Ptolemy, directing them likewise to compel the Jews, but to show mercy to those who obeyed them and did what they wanted.
Those who were unwilling to turn to pagan beliefs were to be put to death. It would break a person's heart to see the people's misery and humiliation.

For they brought forward two women who had circumcised their sons. They hung their sons from their breasts and paraded the women throughout the city. Finally, they took them up and threw them down from the wall.

Others fled secretly to caves to observe the Sabbath there. People came and reported them to Philip, and his men went and burned them, because they were afraid to defend themselves on the glorious Sabbath day.

I therefore ask all who read this book not to be afraid, alarmed, or shaken by what has happened to us. Instead, consider that the judgment that came upon us was not intended for our destruction, but for the discipline of our people.
For this too is a sign of great kindness: they were not left to act wickedly for a long time, but fell under many punishments.
For the Lord has not treated us as he does other nations, with whom he is patient until their sins reach their full measure, and then repays them with torment.
Instead, he punishes us now so that he will not torment us at the end.
For this reason, he has never withdrawn his mercy from us. He does indeed discipline us with punishments, but he has not abandoned his people.
But what has been said up to this point is enough as a reminder. Let us now return to the narrative.
Eleazar, the chief of the scribes, an old man whose face was pleasing and very handsome, was being forced to eat pork.
But he chose a death of suffering full of glory rather than to live a short time in shame. He gladly came forward and surrendered himself to suffering and torture.
This is how steadfast people ought to surrender themselves rather than be defiled by eating anything forbidden, because of the life and hope awaiting them.

Those whom the king had appointed to conduct interrogations and inflict unjust floggings took the honored Eleazar aside privately, because they had known him for a long time. They urged him to bring sacrificial meat suitable for him, prepared for his own use, and eat it, pretending and agreeing to say that he was eating sacrificial meat in obedience to the king’s command.
By doing this, he would escape death, and because of their longstanding friendship with him, he would be treated mercifully.

But he formed a courageous and noble resolve, worthy of his old age, his honored years, his learning, and the godly discipline he had followed since childhood. He answered, “Quickly, without delay, escort me and send me to Sheol!
For it would not be fitting at my age to pretend and put on a false appearance. Many young people would then say that Eleazar, a ninety-year-old man, had turned to paganism.
Because of my pretense, and for the sake of my brief remaining life, they would go astray and perish, while I would become an object of disgrace, laughter, mockery, and contempt in my old age.
Even if I wished to escape this temporary death at human hands, I cannot escape the hands of God, either in life or in death.
Therefore, by departing from this world resolutely and courageously, I will give my old age the honor it deserves.

I will leave the young an example of courage and strength, and encourage them to give themselves up gladly to suffering, torture, and death for the sake of the pure, holy, and glorious law.” When he had said this, they immediately led him away and brought him to be tortured and afflicted.
Those who shortly before had acted as his friends turned hostile because of these words he had spoken. They thought he had spoken them arrogantly and boastfully, and they began to flog him.

When he was close to dying under the blows, he groaned and said, “It is clear to the Lord, who possesses holy knowledge, that although I could have escaped this death, here I am enduring suffering, blows, and bodily pain. Yet in my soul I rejoice that I endure these things for the sake of his law and out of reverence for him.”

After saying these things, he departed from this world. Through his death he left not only the young but many of the people a model and example of courage and strength, and a glorious remembrance and memorial.

It also happened that seven brothers were arrested with their mother. The king was trying to force them to eat unclean pork, and whips and every kind of instrument of torture and suffering were brought and placed before them.
One of them, who was their leader, answered the king, “What are you asking to learn from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the law of our ancestors.”
When the king heard this, he became very angry and ordered a frying pan and cauldrons to be heated.
When they had greatly enraged him, he ordered that the tongue of their leader be cut out and the extremities of all his limbs cut off, while his mother and brothers stood watching him.

When all his limbs had been mutilated, he ordered them to bring him and throw him, still alive, onto a pan over the fire. As a strong smell of burning rose from his body, his brothers and their mother urged one another to die courageously.
“Look, the Lord God sees, and he truly takes comfort in us, as Moses said in his song: ‘He takes comfort in his servants.’”

When the first had reached his end and departed from this world, they brought the second to be mocked and flogged. They tore off the hair of his head together with the skin, and asked him whether he would eat before his whole body was mutilated.
He answered in the language of his ancestors, “I will not eat.” So they killed him too with the same torture.
When he was close to death, he said, “You wicked man, you are releasing us from this temporary life. But the King of the ages, for whose law we are dying, will raise us to everlasting life.”
After this they brought the third and mocked and tortured him. The king ordered them to cut out his tongue, and he immediately stuck out his tongue and gladly stretched out his hands as well.
He answered courageously, “I received these from the one who dwells in heaven, and for the sake of his law I gladly surrender them. I hope to receive them back from him again.”
The king himself and those with him were amazed at the young man’s courage of soul, and at how he neither feared nor paid the slightest regard to the floggings and tortures.
When this one had died, they brought the fourth, and they afflicted and tortured him too.

When he was close to death, he answered, “It is better to die under suffering inflicted by human beings, because of the hope of resurrection to life from God in the world to come. But for you there will be no resurrection to life.”
When this one had died, they brought the fifth and flogged and afflicted him.

But he looked at the king and said to him, “You have authority over human beings, and although you yourself are mortal, you do whatever you please. But do not think that our people have been abandoned by God.”
“Wait, and you will see the sovereign power of his greatness, and how he will torment you and your descendants afterward.”

After this they brought the sixth. When he was close to death, he spoke and said, “Do not delude yourself with empty notions. We are suffering these things on our own account, because we have sinned against our God. For this reason we have become an object of wonder and praise.”
But do not think that you will prevail, since you have chosen to stand against God.”

Their mother, however, is especially praiseworthy and deserves to be remembered with blessing. Although she saw all seven of her sons perish in a single day, she endured it joyfully because of the hope laid up with the Lord.

She pleaded with each one of them, saying in their ancestral language, “My son, have pity on me.” She was filled with a courageous spirit and fervently stirred her womanly thoughts to a man’s resolve. As she implored them, she said to them, “My sons,
I do not know how you came to be in my womb. It was not I who gave you life and breath, nor was it I who fashioned the form and appearance of each of you.

Rather, it was the Creator of the world, who formed the generations of humanity and searches all their intentions and thoughts. In his mercy he will give you breath and life again, because you have surrendered your bodies to destruction for the sake of his holy laws.”

When Antiochus saw that he was being scorned and despised by the words of the taunting woman, he ignored her and pretended not to hear. While the young man stood there, he not only pleaded with him and tried to persuade him with words, but also swore many oaths to him: if he would obey him and turn away from the convictions of his ancestors, he would make him very wealthy, make him his friend, and entrust him with the affairs of the kingdom.
But when the young man paid no attention and would not yield to his words, the king summoned his mother and urged her to advise her son so that he would not die.
After he had said a great deal to her, she said, “I will persuade him.”

She fell at her son’s feet and pleaded with him, mocking the tyrant and outcast as she said to him in their ancestral language, “My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, nursed you for three years, raised you, and brought you to this stage of life.
I beg you, my son, look at heaven and earth and everything in them. Understand and see that God made them from what did not exist, and that the human race also came into being in this way.

So do not be afraid of this condemned man. Instead, prove yourself equal to your brothers and accept death, so that through the mercy that will again be shown to you, I may receive you back together with your brothers.”
While she stood there pleading with him, the young man spoke and said, “What are you waiting for? I will not obey the king’s command. I obey the law of our ancestors, which was given through Moses.
But you, who have schemed and inflicted so many evils on the Hebrews, will not escape from God’s hands.
For we are suffering these things because of our sins.
Our Lord God has been angry with us for a short time to rebuke and discipline us, but he will again be reconciled to his servants.
But you, wicked, unclean man, outcast of all humanity, do not exalt yourself and boast with empty hope against God’s servants.
For you will not escape the judgment of God, who rules over all.

For my brothers, who endured a brief, momentary affliction, will be with God in the life of light, in the glory of his kingdom. But you, under God’s just judgment, will receive the repayment for your deeds that you deserve.

Like my brothers, I surrender my life and body for the sake of the law of our ancestors. I ask God to be reconciled soon with our people and forgive them, and that through torments and tortures you may be called to account and acknowledge that he alone is God.”
And may the wrath of the Most High, which has justly come upon our whole people, come to rest with me and my brothers.”
When the king heard these things, he became extremely angry and afflicted and tortured him more cruelly and bitterly than his brothers.
But he departed from the world undefiled, trusting completely in the Lord.
Last of all, their mother also died.
This is enough to say about the interrogations, tortures, and great and severe floggings.

Judas Maccabeus and those with him secretly entered the villages and gathered their fellow countrymen and those who had remained faithful to the law of Judaism. They assembled and numbered about six thousand men.
They asked the Lord to look upon the people who were being trampled by so many, and also to have mercy on the temple that had been defiled by the wicked,
and to rescue the city that was being destroyed and was close to becoming a wilderness. They asked him also to look upon the slain, whose blood had been shed for no reason,
and to remember the innocent children who had perished unjustly, and the blasphemies uttered against his name, and to rise up against them in zealous anger.

When Maccabeus had become established and strong, together with the company accompanying him, he struck fear and terror into all the nations. For God’s anger had turned away and had become mercy toward them.
He would make sudden attacks and destroy towns and villages. He seized the places near them, won battles, and killed many.
He attacked especially at night and crushed many, and his valor was spoken of and became famous everywhere.

When Philip saw that Maccabeus was growing increasingly powerful and renowned and was winning all his battles, he wrote to Ptolemy, the ruler and governor of Syria and Phoenicia, asking him to support the king’s interests.

Ptolemy immediately commissioned Nicanor son of Patroclus, who was one of his leading friends, and sent him with about twenty thousand troops to go and wipe out the entire Jewish people. He also sent Gorgias with him, a commander and leader experienced in warfare.
Nicanor had promised and pledged to the king that he would bring two thousand talents into the royal treasury from the sale of Jewish captives.

He immediately sent word to the city on the seacoast, inviting its people to come and buy the Jews. He promised to give ninety people for one talent, without considering or anticipating the judgment of God Almighty that was about to overtake him.
People came and informed Judas of Nicanor's approach and told him about the entire army with him.
When the Jews heard this, many of them were afraid and began to doubt God’s righteous judgment, and they began fleeing in every direction.
Others sold what they had left. But all of them together begged the Lord to rescue them from the hands of the wicked Nicanor, who had sold them before he had even come and seen them,
if not for their own sake, then for the sake of the covenant he had made with their ancestors and for the sake of his great, holy, and glorious name that had been invoked over them.

Judas Maccabeus gathered those who were with him, numbering six thousand men. He appealed to them and encouraged them not to fear the battles or be alarmed and shaken by the great numbers of Gentiles who had come against them unjustly.

He said to them, “Look and see the disgrace unjustly inflicted on the holy place at their hands. Commit yourselves and fight bravely.” He also reminded them of the disgrace and mockery the city had suffered at their hands, and of their abolition of the ancestral laws.

He said to them, “They trust in weapons and physical strength, but we trust in the Lord our God, the Almighty, who has the power to overthrow not only our enemies but the whole world with the breath of his mouth.”
He also reminded them of the deliverances their ancestors had experienced in their own times, and of the deliverance in the days of Sennacherib, when one hundred eighty-five thousand perished.

He also recalled the battle against the Galatians: how they had attacked them fiercely with eighty thousand troops, together with another forty thousand Macedonians who had come to help them, and how they had gone out against them with a small force and defeated them because of the help from heaven that was with them.
When they heard these things, they were encouraged, strengthened, and emboldened, and bravely committed themselves to defending their law and their country. He divided the army into four divisions.
He appointed his brothers Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan as commanders and leaders, each over one of the divisions, and entrusted fifteen hundred men to each of them.

He also instructed Eleazar to read the holy law to the people, and gave the signal for deliverance: “God’s help.” He himself was the commander and leader of the first division, and he began to fight against Nicanor.

God Almighty became their helper from heaven, and he killed about nine thousand of the enemy. They cut off the hands, blinded the eyes, and mutilated the limbs of a large part of the enemy’s army. Those who remained of their entire army fled.
They took all the wealth of those who had come to buy them. They pursued the enemy a long way, but then returned because they were in a hurry.
for the time of Sabbath eve was approaching. For this reason they did not continue pursuing them.

They plundered and took everything the enemy had with them, including their weapons, and returned to observe the Sabbath, giving thanks and greatly praising the Lord, who had delivered them that day and had begun to show them mercy.
After the Sabbath, they distributed some of their plunder to the afflicted, the poor, the orphans, and the widows. They divided the rest among themselves and the young men who were with them.
After doing this, they all cried out and prayed before the merciful Lord that he would remain gracious to his servants to the very end.

Timothy and Bacchides attacked them again, but they killed more than thirty thousand of the attackers. They conquered and captured large, strong fortresses and took and distributed a great deal of plunder. They gave shares to the orphans, widows, and poor among the people, and also to the elderly.
They collected all the enemy’s weapons and stored them in designated places. They brought the rest of the plunder to Jerusalem, to the leaders of the people.
Timothy’s men had killed a certain wicked man who had caused the Jews great distress.

When they came to their own land, they celebrated their victory in battle. They brought Callisthenes and those with him and burned them in a single house, because they had burned the sacred gates and fled. They received the punishment their evil and unjust deeds deserved.
Now the guilty and unclean Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants with him to buy the Jews,

He was humbled and fell before those whom he had considered inferior to himself, through the power and help of God, who was with them. He abandoned his splendid clothing and fled like a slave, going to Antioch in distress and great shame because of the destruction of his army.

He who had promised the Romans that he would pay them tribute from the spoils of Jerusalem now proclaimed that the Jews had God as their helper, and that for this reason they could not be defeated, because they followed his commandments.
At that same time, King Antiochus happened to be returning from Persia in shame and great frustration.

For he had gone down to the place called the city of Persia, intending to capture the city and plunder the temple of idols there. When the inhabitants of that land saw this, they gathered against him in great force and defeated the whole army with him. When he saw that he had been defeated, he turned back in shame with his entire army.
When Antiochus was close to reaching Batnan, they informed him about what had happened to Nicanor and Timothy.

When he heard this, he became furious and was greatly carried away by his anger. He intended to come and inflict on the Jews everything that had been done to him in Persia. He ordered his charioteer to drive with great haste so that he could arrive quickly. He said, “I will uproot Jerusalem, the city of the Jews, and make it a dwelling place for the nations.”

But immediately the judgment of the Lord God, the Mighty One of Israel, overtook him and struck him with a bitter, invisible affliction. Before he had finished speaking, a bitter and severe pain seized his internal organs and intestines.
He justly repaid the man who had tortured and tormented the internal organs of others with pain, affliction, and many tortures.

Although all these things had happened to him, he still raged and remained arrogant in his thinking. He was filled with anger against the Jews that blazed like fire, and he ordered his charioteer to drive still faster and more swiftly. In the violent rush of his chariot, he was thrown out and suffered a severe and painful fall, and all his limbs were broken.

The man who, a little earlier, had thought he could command even the waves of the sea, because his arrogance exceeded that of all other people, and could bring down all the lofty mountains, now lay on the ground, plainly displaying the power of God to everyone.

The wicked man's suffering was so severe that worms crawled out of his body. While he was still alive, his flesh peeled away and fell off, and the stench of his body was so foul that no one in his army could endure it.
No one could approach the man who, a little earlier, had thought he could command even the stars of heaven, because of his foul stench.
From this point he began to abandon his excessive arrogance. Humbled, he turned toward knowledge of the truth, because he was being tormented and afflicted by every kind of scourge from heaven.
When he could no longer endure his own stench, he spoke and said, “It is right for a person to submit to God, and not, being mortal, to entertain thoughts against God.”
The wicked man prayed and pleaded with the Lord, who would no longer have mercy on him, saying:
“As for the holy city, which I was hurrying to overthrow and make a dwelling place for all the nations, I will rebuild it and enclose it.”

Concerning the Jews, he said, “I had intended that they should not even receive burial, but that they, together with their wives and children, should become food for the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth. I will make them all Athenians.”

“As for the holy temple, which I previously plundered, I will adorn and decorate it with every kind of ornament. I will provide many times as many sacred vessels, and I will pay from my own resources every expense incurred for sacrifices and offerings.”
“After these things, I will also become a Jew myself, and wherever I go, I will proclaim the greatness of God's dominion.”
Despite all this, he found no relief from his pains, for God's just judgment had overtaken him. When he despaired of his life, he wrote the Jews a letter of supplication as follows:
“Antiochus, king and governor, to the worthy Jews, my fellow citizens: greetings and peace.”
“May you and your children be in good health. I pray and ask this of God in heaven, in whose great goodness I place my hope.”

“When I became ill, I remembered your interests, intending to grant you honor and great relief, because my heart burned with love for you. As I was coming up from the land of Persia, when I was close to arriving, I fell into a severe and painful illness. It seemed right to me to attend to your interests above everything else.”
For I do not know what will happen to me, but I hope to recover from this illness.
I saw that my father too, whenever he went up to the upper regions, made known who would succeed him,
so that, if anything unfortunate happened, the people of the country would know who was to take his place and would not fight one another.

So I too, when I saw that the nobles of my kingdom were ready and watching over the kingdom, waiting to see what would happen, made my decision known and appointed my son Antiochus as king. He is the one whom I entrusted to you many times when I went up to the upper regions. I have also written to him what is written here.
I ask and urge you to remember my kindness toward you, and that all of you together, and each one of you individually, maintain friendship and brotherhood with my son.
For I know that he agrees with my intentions in everything and will treat you with gentleness and friendship.
But Antiochus, the murderer, the wicked man and blasphemer, died among the mountains in a foreign land, amid afflictions, torments, and severe tortures, just as he himself had tortured others.
Philip, his foster brother, took his body to bring it back with him. But as he approached, he became afraid of Antiochus's son Antiochus, fled, and went to Ptolemy son of Philometor in Egypt.
Maccabeus and those with him, with the help of the Lord who was with them, took possession of the temple and the city.
They demolished the shrines and the idol temple that the Gentiles had built in its streets.

They purified the temple and made another altar. They put stones through fire and took fire from them, and offered sacrifices and an offering after two years. They also prepared lamps, lampstands, incense, and the bread of the Presence.

When they had done this, they fell on their faces and prayed, asking the Lord that they might never again encounter these afflictions and tortures. But even if they happened to sin, they asked that he himself would discipline them mercifully and that they would not be handed over to uncircumcised, unclean, and blasphemous nations.
It happened that the temple was purified on the very same day on which it had been defiled by the nations: the twenty-fifth of the month called First Kanun.

With great joy and rejoicing, they celebrated a festival for eight days each year, like the Festival of Booths. They remembered that, only a short time earlier, during the Festival of Booths, they had been living in mountains and caves and grazing like wild animals.
For this reason they held palm branches and praised and gave thanks to the one who had delivered them and given them strength to purify and sanctify his place.
They all agreed together that the entire congregation of the Jews should observe these days every year.
Such was the end and death of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes.
Now let us also speak about Antiochus Eupator, his wicked son. We will speak briefly about the many evils that occurred in the war.
For when he succeeded to his father's kingdom, he put Lysias in charge of his affairs, the man who had previously been appointed chief and governor over Syria and Phoenicia.
Ptolemy, who was called Macedon, maintained friendship with the Jews. He was distressed over the wrongs done to them and wanted to be at peace with them.

Some of his friends went and accused him before Eupator. They constantly called him a traitor because Philometor had entrusted Cyprus to him, but he had abandoned it and gone over to Antiochus Epiphanes. Because of this, he had neither high rank nor honor in the kingdom. When he saw that all these things had happened to him, he took his own life with poison.
Gorgias took his place as chief and governor. He gathered many nations around him and was continually at war with the Jews.
The Edomites also joined him. They came and fought against the nearby fortresses and greatly harassed the Jews. They welcomed those who fled from Jerusalem and prepared to fight against Israel.
But Judas Maccabeus and his followers cried out, prayed, and earnestly asked God to be their helper. Then they formed ranks and marched against the fortresses of the Edomites.
They fought against them fiercely and courageously, exerted their strength, and conquered them. They killed everyone who fought on the walls, killing about twenty thousand.
About nine thousand escaped from them and entered two large, strongly fortified strongholds.

Judas Maccabeus went to the places where the need was urgent, leaving Simon, Joseph, Zacchaeus, and many of his men to remain and fight against the fortresses and capture them. After Maccabeus had left that place,
some of the men with Simon, out of love for money, accepted bribes from those in the fortresses. They took seventy thousand in silver from them and allowed some of them to escape.
When Maccabeus learned of the matter, he gathered the leaders of the people and rebuked them for having sold their brothers for money and let their enemies go.
He killed those who had acted as traitors and quickly captured the strongholds.
Although he had only a few men, he killed more than twenty thousand in their [?] strongholds.

Now Timothy, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, gathered a large and powerful foreign army, including the warriors of Asia and many cavalrymen. He was coming to Jerusalem, planning to devastate Judea and take everyone in it captive.
When Maccabeus and his men heard that he was approaching, they devoted themselves to crying out and praying before God, with dust scattered on their heads and sackcloth wrapped around their waists.
They threw themselves down before the altar and begged the Lord to be reconciled to them, to help them, to fight their enemies, and to stand against those who hated them, as the Law says.
When they had finished their prayers and petitions, they took up their weapons and marched confidently against them. When they reached the battlefield, they stopped and kept to themselves.
When day broke and the sun rose, both sides began to fight. The Jews trusted in the Lord God, who had given them victory and deliverance, while the others trusted in the commanders of their army.
When the battle became great and fierce, five splendid and glorious riders appeared from heaven to their enemies, with their horses outfitted in gold, helping the Jews.

They took Judas Maccabeus between them, sheltered him with the wings of their armor, and protected him from every blow. They hurled arrows and javelins at their enemies. When the enemies saw these things, their eyes were dazzled and all their strength gave way.
They killed twenty thousand five hundred of their infantry and six hundred cavalrymen.
Timothy fled to the fortress called Gazara, which was exceedingly strong and secure. It was the prison of Chaereas, who had formerly been chief and governor there.
Maccabeus and his men confidently laid siege to the stronghold for four days.
Because those living in it trusted in its strength and its defenses, they heaped insults and abuse on Judas Maccabeus and his men, speaking filthy and disgusting words to them.

As dawn approached on the fifth day, twenty young men from among those with Maccabeus were filled with zeal and blazed with anger because of their blasphemy. They ran at the fortress and leaped forward bravely like enraged wild animals, killing everyone who fell into their hands.

Others also leaped up and climbed, setting fire to those in the towers. They kindled a fire and burned the blasphemers alive. Still others broke down the gates, and in this way they entered the city and captured it.
They found Timothy hiding in a pit and killed him there, along with his brother Chaereas and Apollonius.
After doing these things, they blessed God with songs of praise and thanksgiving, because he had shown great kindness to Israel and given it victory.
A short time later, when Lysias, the king’s guardian and relative, heard about everything that had happened, he became furious and deeply embittered.
He gathered an army of more than eighty thousand and many cavalrymen, and marched against the Jews. He planned to make the city a settlement for the Gentiles,
to make the temple a place for collecting money like the other temples of idols, and to dissolve and abolish the high priesthood.
He did not remember or keep before his eyes the greatness and judgment of God. Instead, he was proud and arrogant, trusting in the size of his army, his thousands of cavalrymen, and his elephants.
He entered Judea and advanced against Beth-zur. He encamped against a large village about ten thousand and five stadia from Jerusalem and began to besiege it.
When Maccabeus and his men heard that he had begun plundering and capturing fortresses, they begged the Lord with weeping and tears to send a good angel to save Israel.

Maccabeus himself was the first to take up his weapons. He also urged and encouraged his companions to help their brothers who were suffering under the oppression of their enemies, and they all marched out courageously together.
While they were still near Jerusalem, their leader appeared to them in white clothing, riding a horse and wearing golden armor. He flashed his weapons and waved them toward them.

Immediately they all raised their voices and blessed the merciful God of heaven. They became firm and courageous in spirit, ready not only to attack human beings but also to overthrow savage beasts and walls of iron.
They went forward confidently, believing that God was merciful to them and was their helper.
They rushed like lions against their enemies and struck down about eleven thousand of them, along with sixteen hundred cavalrymen. The rest fled.
Many of them fled naked and wounded. Lysias himself also escaped by fleeing in great disgrace.

When Lysias came to his senses, he reflected on what had happened to him. He considered the matter and said that the Hebrews could not be defeated because the mighty God was helping them, and he sent word to them.
He sought to establish friendship with them and said that he would also persuade the king to be their friend.
Maccabeus agreed to everything Lysias requested, because he wanted what would be beneficial to happen. And everything Maccabeus wrote and sent to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king granted them.
The letters Lysias wrote to the Jews were as follows: “Lysias to the assembly of the Jews, greetings.
John and Absalom, whom you sent, delivered the letters and made requests concerning what was written in them.
“I presented to the king what needed to be brought before him, and he granted what it was right to grant.
“If, then, you maintain your friendship with us, I will be the source of every benefit for you.
“Concerning the matters you wrote about, I have written and sent word that everything should be done for you as you wish.
“In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the twenty-fourth of Second Tishri.”
The king’s letter arrived, written as follows: “King Antiochus to his brother Lysias: Greetings.
Since my father departed to the gods, I want our kingdom to be free from unrest. For this reason I have written concerning the welfare of the Jews.

For we have heard that they were unwilling to submit to my father’s intention regarding pagan worship, but wish to remain faithful to their own laws. For this reason they are asking that they be allowed to keep their laws.
We too want this people to be free from unrest and fear, their temple to be given back to them, and their lives and conduct to follow the laws and customs of their ancestors.
You will therefore do well to send word to them and give them your pledge, so that, when they see our disposition toward them, they may conduct all their affairs happily and peacefully.”
The king’s letter to the Jewish people was written as follows: “King Antiochus to the elders of the Jews and the rest of the Jews, greetings.
“May you be in good health, as we wish. We too are well.
Menelaus has informed us that you want to carry on your work and business peacefully and to conduct your lives according to your laws.
“We too have given a pledge of peace and have pardoned offenses until the end of the month of Nisan.
Let the Jews therefore follow their laws as before, and let no one threaten any of them over any matter whatsoever.”
“I have sent Menelaus to inform you of these very things.”
Stay well. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth of Nisan.
The Romans also sent a letter to the Jews, written as follows: “Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, elders of the Romans, to the assembly of the Jews, greetings.
We too approve of everything that Lysias, the king’s relative, has granted you.

Furthermore, concerning everything he spoke to the king about on your behalf, send men so that these things may be done for you and we may satisfy you in everything you desire, for we are now preparing to come to Antioch.”
Therefore hurry to send us someone who can inform us how you are doing.
In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth of Nisan.
When these matters had taken place, Lysias departed and went to the king, and the Jews returned to their work and business.
But the chiefs and governors in the regions—Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, Hieronymus, Ramphon, and Nicanor, along with the Cypriots—would not let them live quietly and rest.

The people of Joppa committed a great act of wickedness in this way: they persuaded the Jews living among them to board boats with their wives and children, although there was neither hostility nor dispute between them.

All the townspeople plotted together and agreed to this, pretending that they wanted to make peace. Without suspecting anything, the Jews went aboard and sat down. They went out, and the townspeople drowned them in the sea, about two hundred people.
When Judas heard about the evil and wickedness inflicted on his fellow Jews, he gave orders to the men with him.

He prayed and cried out to God, the righteous judge, and attacked the murderers of their brothers. They burned their harbor at night, together with the ships in it, and killed those they found aboard them.
When the townspeople became aware of it, they shut the gates. He turned back and withdrew, for he intended to attack them again and was planning to destroy Joppa together with its inhabitants.
He also learned that the people of Jamnia intended to do the same to the Jews living there.
He went there at night and burned their harbor with everything in it, so that the glow of the fire as it burned could be seen as far away as Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.
They moved about nine stadia from there and were advancing against Timothy when Arabs attacked them, about five thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry.

When the battle and fierce fighting took place, Judas and his men prevailed because of the help God gave them. After their defeat, the leaders asked Judas to give them his pledge, promising that they would also give him livestock.
Judas thought that they would be useful to him in many matters and agreed to make peace with them. When they had received his pledge, they went back to their tents.
Judas attacked a strong city, enclosed and fortified by its walls, where people of many nations lived. Its name was Caspin.

Because its inhabitants trusted in the strength of its walls and the abundant weapons stored inside it, they behaved with extreme arrogance, blaspheming and insulting Judas and his men and speaking filthy, improper words to them.

But Judas and his men prayed and cried out to God, the mighty ruler of the ages, who had overthrown the walls of Jericho in Joshua’s days without stones, siege engines, or human skill. They advanced and hurled themselves against the wall like wild animals and overthrew it.
By God's will they captured the city and killed so many people in it that the nearby lake, which measured about two stadia, was entirely mixed with blood.
They set out from there and traveled about seven hundred and fifty stadia, entering Charax to join the Jews called the Tobians.
They found Timothy there without an army, his hands hanging helplessly because he had no troops with him. He did, however, still have a garrison in a large, strong fortress.
Dositheus and Sosipater, commanders and leaders among Maccabeus's men, went and killed the men Timothy had left in the fortresses, more than ten thousand men.

Maccabeus gathered the army that was with him, divided them into units, and appointed a commander over each unit. He then advanced against Timothy, who had come against them with an army of one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.

When Timothy heard about Judas and his men, he sent their wives, their children, and all their baggage to the town called Carna. The town was strong and fortified and could not easily be captured or plundered, because its approaches were narrow on every side.

When Judas's advance force appeared, fear and trembling fell upon the enemies by the will of God Almighty, who appeared to them. They all took to flight, each fleeing in his own direction, so that they ran into one another and climbed over one another, stabbing one another and wounding their limbs because their swords were drawn.
Judas pursued them fiercely, killing those wicked men. He killed about thirty thousand of them.

Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus, Sosipater, and their men, and they captured him. He begged and pleaded with them to spare his life. They, however, because many of them had brothers and relatives in his custody—
He promised them that he would release those men alive. Out of concern for their brothers' lives, they were reluctant to refuse him, and they spared his life.
Judas Maccabeus marched against the place called Carna and Atargatis, and killed twenty-five thousand there.

After these men had been defeated and killed, Judas rallied his army and marched against Ephron, a strong city where Lysias lived. A large gathering of people from the nations and strong young men fought fiercely from its walls with arrows, spears, and every kind of weapon.

Judas and his men prayed and cried out to God, who has the power to crush and break all the strength of their enemies. He delivered the city into their hands, and they entered it, captured it, and killed about twenty-five thousand people in it.
From there they set out and went to Beth-shan, which is about six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.
The Jews who lived there testified concerning the people of the city that they treated them very kindly and held them in honor.
Judas and his men acknowledged their kindness and greeted them peacefully. From there they went to Jerusalem to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread.
After Pentecost they marched against Gorgias, the ruler and governor of the Idumeans.
He came out against them with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.
When they began fighting, a few men among the Idumeans fell.

Dositheus, one of the Tobians, a cavalryman and a powerful man, seized Gorgias by his cloak and forcibly dragged him along, because he wanted to bring that guilty man in alive. But one of Gorgias's soldiers, a Thracian, came at him, struck him on the shoulder, and cut it off. Gorgias escaped and went to Samaria.
Azariah and his men were fighting and killing with great intensity. Judas cried out to the mighty Lord to help them, and he himself was the first to charge against the enemy.
Singing hymns to the ancestral tune, he began to kill them. Gorgias and his men were defeated and fled.
Judas and his army set out from there and came to the city of Adullam. As the Sabbath was approaching, they purified themselves according to their custom and observed the Sabbath where they were.
The next day they came to Judas and asked to gather the bodies of those who had fallen and bury them in their ancestral tombs.

Under the clothing of each of them they found hidden gold from the idols of the people of Jamnia, things the law had forbidden the Jews to keep. Everyone understood and was convinced that this was why those men had fallen.
They all blessed God and gave thanks for his righteous judgment, for he brings hidden things out and reveals them openly.

They all began to pray and plead with God that this would not be counted against them as a deadly sin. Judas, the warrior, urged and pleaded with all the people to guard themselves and beware of sins. He told them, "You have seen with your own eyes what happened to these men."

He imposed a levy on all the people, requiring them to contribute silver. He collected three thousand silver coins and sent them to Jerusalem so that sacrifices could be offered on their behalf. He acted rightly and justly because of his hope in the resurrection from the dead.
For if he had not been expecting and hoping for the resurrection from the dead, it would have been pointless and foolish for anyone to pray and offer sacrifices on behalf of the dead.

For he was looking ahead and waiting for the reward, hope, and rest prepared for those who die in righteousness. For this reason he sent the money so that atonement could be made for the sins of those who had died.
In the one hundred and forty-ninth year, Antiochus Eupator came against the Jews.

With him was Lysias, who had been put in charge of affairs. He had with him an army drawn from many nations: one hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots reinforced with shields for battle.

Menelaus also went and joined them. He pleaded with Antiochus and begged him to march against his country and his fellow citizens to destroy them, not to help them, because he hoped to go and establish himself in authority.

But the Lord, the King of kings, stirred up Antiochus's anger against the guilty Menelaus, because Lysias had informed him that Menelaus was the cause of all the troubles. He ordered them to take him to Aleppo and put him to death there.
There was a tower there, fifty cubits high, which was full of ashes. It had wheels and was moved by a mechanical device.
There they confined the plunderer of the temple, the perpetrator of all these evils.
By this torture the guilty and wicked Menelaus died. He was not considered worthy even of burial in the ground, and he received his just punishment.
For he had committed evil acts against the altar, where the sacred fire and ashes were. For this reason he met his death in ashes.
The king was still angry and bitterly hostile toward the Jews, and he was planning to inflict far more harm on them than his father had.

When Judas learned of the king's approach and his plans, he instructed the people to be vigilant in prayer day and night and to cry out to God to help them and deliver them, now and always, from the power of the nations,

who wanted to separate them from the law, their country, and the holy temple. He was not to allow the people, who had enjoyed relief and rest for only a short time, to be enslaved to wicked and uncircumcised nations.
