They all prayed and cried out in this way, pleading with the merciful God with much weeping. They fasted for three days, continually lying facedown and crying out. After three days Judas appealed to them and encouraged them to eat.

Judas went alone to the elders and consulted with them. He said, “Before the king's army enters Judea and they conquer and exhaust the city's strength, let us go out and take action and put everything in order with God's help.”

He entrusted the direction of affairs to God, the Creator of the world, and urged those with him to fight bravely and surrender their lives, even to death, for the law, the temple, the city, the country, and their fellow people. He gathered his whole army, and they made preparations at Modein.

He gave those with him “God's deliverance” as their signal. Taking selected, strong young men with him, he advanced against the camp and attacked the king's quarters at night. He killed about three thousand men there and smashed and brought down the largest of the elephants, together with all its equipment.
They filled the whole camp with terror and confusion, and returned from there with delight and joy.
They did this as dawn was approaching, because the Lord’s power and help were overshadowing them.
When the king experienced and saw the strength and courage of the Jews, he wanted to subdue them by skill and deceit.
He sent a force against Beth-zur, the Jews' stronghold. They fought against it but were defeated and suffered heavy losses.
Meanwhile, Judas kept sending supplies to those inside the fortresses.
Rhodocus went from the land of Judea and disclosed their secrets to their enemies. An order was given, and they found him and killed him.
The king came against Beth-zur again, exchanged pledges, and departed.

He advanced against Judas's men and fought with them, but he was defeated and withdrew. Suspecting that Philip, whom he had appointed to oversee affairs in Antioch, wanted to rebel against him, he made peace with the Jews, bound himself to them, swore an oath to them, and established friendship with them. He offered sacrifices, bestowed great honor on the temple, and also showed kindness to the country.
He received Maccabeus with great affection and left Hegemonides as chief and governor from Ptolemais to Gezer.
He went to Ptolemais. The people of Ptolemais were distressed over the covenant he had made with the Jews. They were extremely angry with him and wanted to annul the covenant he had made with them.
Lysias came before the tribunal, brought them relief, persuaded them, and pacified them. He then set out from there for Antioch. Such was the course of the king's expedition and his return.
After three years, Demetrius son of Seleucus came against the people of Judah. He entered the harbor of Alas [?] with a large, powerful, and heavily armed army.
To take possession of the whole land, because he had killed Antiochus and Lysias, his chief steward.

Now Alcimus, who had formerly been high priest and had thoroughly defiled himself during the time of intermingling, considered his situation and saw that he had no hope at all and could not even approach the altar.

He went to King Demetrius in the year one hundred and fifty-one and brought him a gold crown, a gold ear of grain, and, along with them, palm branches from the temple. That day, however, he remained quiet.
When Alcimus found an opportunity for his insolence and wickedness, Demetrius invited him to a meeting and asked him, “What intention or plan makes the Jews so bold?” He answered him:

“Those who are called the illustrious among the Jews, over whom Judas Maccabeus has been appointed, stir up rebellion, provoke unrest, and intensify the war. They will not allow the kingdom to have peace.
For this reason I too have left my ancestral honor, the high priesthood, and here I have come before you for the second time.

For I care about the king’s affairs and take responsibility for them, and secondly, I am concerned for our own people. For I see the arrogance and pride of those I mentioned earlier, how they oppress our people and do not allow them even a little rest.
Now that you have learned these things, O king, take responsibility for our land and our afflicted and unfortunate people, in keeping with your compassion toward all humanity.”
For as long as Judas lives, there can be no peace in our land.
When the king heard these words from him, the king’s friends, because they were hostile to Judas, immediately inflamed Demetrius’s anger against him.
King Demetrius immediately summoned Nicanor, who had been appointed commander of the elephants, a chief and leader.
He gave him letters and sent him away, ordering him to kill Judas, scatter those who were with him, and establish Alcimus as high priest of the great and glorious temple.
The Gentiles who had fled from the land of Judah came and joined Nicanor. They took pleasure and rejoiced in the suffering and distress that had come upon the people of Judah.

When the people of Judah heard about Nicanor’s arrival and the hostility of the Gentiles, they threw dust on their heads and cried out and prayed before the one who had always been their helper and who always openly delivered his inheritance.
Judas ordered them to equip themselves with their weapons, and they immediately set out and met them at a village called Dessau.
Simon, Judas’s brother, suddenly attacked Nicanor, but because they had rushed against him, they were thrown into panic by him.

But when Nicanor heard about the courage and victories of Judas and his men, and how they gave their lives for their people and their country, he did not want to settle the matter through slaughter and bloodshed.
Instead, he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to exchange pledges of friendship.
When Judas heard this, he consulted the people. They considered it together and saw that Nicanor’s words were peaceful, and it was agreed that he should make peace with him.
They fixed a day on which to meet one another. Each of them wore clothing wrapped around him over his weapons.

Judas ordered his army to equip themselves with their weapons. They stood ready at the places where they feared that some sudden treachery might occur. The two met one another with great friendliness and spoke words of peace.
Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing wrong. He dismissed the Gentiles who had gathered around him.
He held Judas in great affection and was always cheerful in his company.
He asked him and persuaded him to marry and have children. So Judas married and took part in ordinary life.

But when Alcimus saw the affection and harmony between Nicanor and Judas, he went to King Demetrius and said to him about Nicanor, “He has turned against your kingdom and all your affairs, for he has made Judas, the enemy of your kingdom, his partner and friend.”

When the king heard the enemy’s slander, he became fiercely angry and wrote harshly to Nicanor about his friendship with Judas. He ordered him to seize Maccabeus, bind him, and send him quickly to Antioch.
When Nicanor heard the letter, he was dismayed and deeply distressed. He did not want to turn against Judas, a man who had done nothing wrong.
Yet he could not defy the king’s command, and he considered what pretext he could use to arrest him.

But when Maccabeus saw that Nicanor’s expression toward him was no longer as it had been before, but was gloomy and different from usual, he realized that Nicanor’s attitude toward him had indeed changed. He gathered a considerable number of his people around him and withdrew from Nicanor.

When Nicanor learned that Judas had prepared himself and strengthened his forces, he entered the great and holy temple while the priests were standing and offering sacrifices, and said to them, “Hand Judas over to me.”
But they swore to him, saying, “We have not seen him, and we do not know where he is.”

He raised his hand toward the temple and swore to them: “Unless you hand Judas over to me in chains, I will turn this temple of God into a wilderness, overthrow the altar, and build a prominent temple to Dionysus in its place.”
After saying all this, he left. But the priests stretched out their hands toward the one who dwells in heaven, pleading and praying to him who had always been his people’s helper. They said:
“You, Lord of all, need nothing. Yet you chose to select a place for your temple, so that your presence might dwell among us.
And now, Lord, holy above all holy ones, preserve forever this place and this undefiled house, which has recently been purified, and shut every mouth of the wicked.”

A man named Razis, one of the elders of Jerusalem, had been reported to Nicanor as a man who loved his city and had an exceptionally good reputation. Because of his good and kindly disposition, he was called the father of the Jews.
For he had long followed the religion and would not allow intermingling among the Jewish people. His soul and body were devoted, in every prayer and petition, to the practices of Judaism.
Nicanor, wishing to show the hatred he held toward the Jews, sent about five hundred of his soldiers to arrest him.
For he said, “When I arrest this man, I will cause the Jews great distress.”

When the crowd arrived and surrounded his courtyard, they tried to force open the gates and burn them with fire. When he saw that they were close to seizing him, he took a sword and stabbed himself in the belly.
For he wished to die as a free man rather than be handed over to wicked and unjust men who would disgrace the dignity of his old age.

But his blow failed because of his haste and agitation. As the crowds entered through the courtyard gates, he leaped up onto the wall bravely and forcefully and threw himself into the midst of the crowds.
When they saw this, they immediately drew back and made room.

While he was still alive and burning with fierce zeal, he sprang to his feet, with much blood flowing from him because his wounds were severe. He ran through the entire crowd and stood on a high rock.

Completely drenched in blood, he pulled out his intestines, held them in both hands, and showed them to the people. He prayed, pleaded, and called upon the one who has authority over life and breath to give them back to him again. Then he departed from this world.
Nicanor heard and learned that Judas and his men were near Samaria, and he planned to attack them by surprise with a large force on the Sabbath day of rest.

But the Jews pleaded with him in great distress, saying, “Do not do this and cruelly destroy people who do not deserve it. Instead, give honor to the great and holy day honored by the Maker and Creator of all.”
But the wicked and impure man asked whether there was a mighty one in heaven who had given the command concerning the Sabbath day.
They answered him, “The living Lord exists, and he is the mighty one in heaven who commanded that the Sabbath day be observed.”
The impure and wicked man replied, “I too am mighty on earth, and I command you to take up arms and carry out the king’s business.” And he was not prevented from carrying out his impure intention.
Nicanor was becoming exalted and puffed up with great pride. He learned that Judas and his men were gathered and ready, and he became still more defiant.
But Judas Maccabeus was hopeful and fully confident that God would bring him deliverance.

He encouraged those with him and told them not to fear the crowds of nations coming against them. He reminded them again of the help they had received from heaven in the past, saying, “Look ahead and await the victory that will come to you from God Almighty.”
He exhorted them from the Law and the Prophets, reminded them of the heroic deeds and struggles they had undertaken in the past, and strengthened and encouraged them.
He stirred up anger and zeal in them, showing them again the wickedness of the nations and the treachery with which they had violated their oath.

Judas armed and equipped each of them, not with spears and shields, but with good words of comfort, encouragement, and strength. He told them of a vision he had seen, worthy of acceptance and belief, and when they heard it, they were all heartened.

This was the account of the vision he had seen: He saw Onias the priest, a fine and good man, modest [?], humble by nature, and gracious and fitting in his speech. From his youth he had followed everything that was right and proper. In the vision he saw this man standing with his hands outstretched, praying for the entire Jewish people.
Then another man appeared to him, distinguished by a noble old age and great glory. His appearance was magnificent, and a splendid majesty rested upon him.
Onias answered and said of him, “This is Jeremiah the prophet, who loves his brothers and earnestly pleads, makes supplication, and prays on behalf of the people and the holy city.”
Jeremiah stretched out his right hand, gave Judas a golden spear, and said to him,
“Receive this spear, a gift from God, with which you will strike and crush all your enemies.”

When Judas’s companions heard these words, they were encouraged by his fine words and greatly strengthened. For these words could strengthen, inspire, and fortify those who heard them and fully prepare the spirits of the young men. They resolved within themselves not to rely on battle formations and military preparations, but to muster all their courage and willingly expose themselves to suffering, with complete determination, for the holy city, the holy temple, and the entire sanctuary.
They were comparatively little concerned about their wives, children, brothers, and families, for their great concern and anxiety were for the holy temple.
Those who remained in the city also experienced no small anguish and distress, fearing that they might become frightened and weakened by the turmoil of battle.

While they were all awaiting the outcome, the enemy advanced and drew up their ranks against them. The elephants were made ready and stood in their formations, and the cavalry also armed themselves and took their positions.

When Judas Maccabeus saw their formations, the strength of the enemy army, their stock of weapons, and the readiness and ferocity of the elephants, he raised his hands to heaven, prayed, and cried out to God, who performs wonders and mighty deeds. For he knew that victory in battle did not depend on weapons, but on whom God wished to grant victory.
As he prayed and pleaded, he said, “You, Lord, sent your angel in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and he killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand in Sennacherib’s camp.
And now, Mighty One who dwells in heaven, send a good angel ahead of us, and let him cast trembling, dread, and terror upon them.
By the strength and greatness of your arm, let those who have come with blasphemy against your holy people fall.” With these words Judas finished.
Nicanor’s men advanced to battle with lyres, harps, and the music of horns.
But Judas’s men charged against them with prayer and supplication.

They fought with their hands, while in their hearts they prayed and cried out to God. They struck down and killed about thirty-five thousand of them, and they were glad and rejoiced over the help God had given them.
When they stopped fighting and returned from battle, rejoicing, giving thanks, and praising God, they learned that Nicanor had fallen in battle along with all the soldiers who accompanied him.
There was trembling and terror in his camp, but Judas’s men gave thanks and blessed the Lord in the language of their ancestors.

Then the man who had devoted his soul and body completely to every hardship for his people and his city, and who had gladly served throughout his life as the leader and commander of his people’s battles, ordered them to cut off Nicanor’s head and his arm together with the shoulder and bring them to Jerusalem.
When Maccabeus came to Jerusalem, he summoned his people and the priests before the altar, and he sent for the men of the citadel.
He showed them the head of the unclean Nicanor and the blasphemer’s hand, which he had raised in arrogance and pride against the temple of God Almighty.
He cut the wicked man’s tongue out of his head, chopped it into small pieces, and ordered it to be given to the birds. His arm he fastened up opposite the temple.
Then they all blessed the Lord who dwells in heaven, crying out, “You are praised, Lord, for you have kept your place pure.”
He fastened the unclean man’s head in a high and conspicuous place opposite the citadel, so that the deliverance wrought by our God could be seen and known by everyone.
They agreed among themselves not to let this day pass as an ordinary day, but to mark it on the thirteenth of Adar, the twelfth month, as it is called in Aramaic, one day before Mordecai’s day.

This, then, is how matters stood concerning Nicanor and everything that happened in those days. From that time onward, the Hebrews possessed and ruled their cities. And now I will bring my account to an end.
If it has been composed well and skillfully, that is what I myself desired. But if it is inadequate and poor, may this be forgiven me.

For just as drinking wine alone or water alone does not delight the soul, but wine mixed with water is pleasant and gives its full benefit to those who drink it, so too the arrangement and composition of an account gladden and delight the hearing of those who read, study attentively, examine, and inquire. Here, then, let the account of these events come to an end.
